questions.explain: b = a copies the reference, not the list — both names point at the same object, so mutating through b is visible through a. This is the number-one production bug with lists passed into functions: the caller's data changes silently. When you need an independent list, say so explicitly with a.copy() or list(a).

questions.code:
def add_item(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add_item(1))
print(add_item(2))
questions.explain: Default values are evaluated once, at def time — every call that omits bucket shares the same list, so state leaks between calls. In production this surfaces as data from one request bleeding into another. The idiom is bucket=None, then 'if bucket is None: bucket = []' inside the function.

Dicts iterate in insertion order (a language guarantee since 3.7), and updating the value of an existing key does not move it — 'a' keeps its original slot. Note insertion order is not sorted order: if you need keys sorted, you must call sorted(d) yourself.

A set keeps exactly one of each value: {'red', 'blue', 'green'} has 3 members. But note what you gave up — iteration order over a set is arbitrary (hash-dependent), so never build user-visible output straight from set iteration; dedupe in order with list(dict.fromkeys(tags)) instead.

choices: TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
questions.explain: Tuple immutability is shallow: the tuple's slots can never be reassigned (t[0] = ... would raise), but the objects inside remain whatever they are — and this list is happily mutable. In production this means a tuple is not a deep-freeze; if it contains a list, anyone holding a reference can still change your 'immutable' record.

s[-4:] means 'from the 4th character from the end, to the end' — 'view'. s[::2] takes every second character starting at index 0: i-t-r-i-w. Slicing never raises for out-of-range bounds and always returns a new string; interviewers love s[::-1] (reverse) and off-by-one negative indices.

With a negative step the slice walks backwards from start toward stop, and the stop index is still excluded: 4, 3, 2 — not 1. [::-1] is the idiomatic full reverse (a new list; the original is untouched, unlike nums.reverse()). Getting the exclusive stop wrong is the classic off-by-one here.

questions.code:
grid = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
snapshot = grid.copy()
snapshot[0].append(7)
snapshot.append([9, 9])
print(grid)
questions.explain: copy() is shallow: the new outer list has its own slots (so appending [9, 9] doesn't touch grid), but those slots point at the same inner lists — mutating snapshot[0] mutates grid[0]. When nested data must be independent, you need copy.deepcopy, and you pay for it: it walks and re-allocates the whole structure.

list.sort() sorts in place and returns None — a deliberate Python convention: mutating methods don't return the object, so you can't mistake them for pure ones. sorted(scores) is the expression form that returns a new list and works on any iterable. 'x = xs.sort()' silently planting None in a variable is a real, common production bug.

Every word has length 3, and Python's sort is stable: elements whose keys compare equal keep their original relative order, so the list comes back untouched. Stability is why multi-key sorting works as 'sort by secondary key first, then by primary' — a favorite interview follow-up.

questions.code:
pairs = [(x, y) for x in range(3) for y in range(2) if x != y]
print(pairs)
questions.explain: Two for clauses nest left-to-right like nested loops: x is the outer loop, y the inner, and the if filters each (x, y) pair — (0,0) and (1,1) are dropped. Reading comprehensions as loops, in clause order, is the fastest way to stop guessing on these.

questions.code:
vals = [x if x % 2 else x * 10 for x in range(5)]
print(vals)
questions.explain: 'A if cond else B' before the for is a per-element transform, not a filter — every x produces a value. x % 2 is 0 (falsy) for even numbers, so evens take the else branch and get multiplied by 10. A trailing 'if' (after the for) would filter instead; confusing the two positions is the classic trap.

choices: Prints 0, prints None, then raises KeyError
Raises KeyError on the first line
questions.explain: get() returns the default (or None) for missing keys and never raises; [] raises KeyError. Choose deliberately in production: get() for genuinely-optional keys, [] when a missing key means the data is broken and you WANT the loud failure — get() everywhere can hide corruption behind quiet Nones.

questions.code:
names = ["Ana", "Bo", "Cy"]
levels = [3, 5]
for i, pair in enumerate(zip(names, levels), start=1):
    print(i, pair)
choices: ValueError: zip() arguments have different lengths
questions.explain: zip stops silently at the shortest input — 'Cy' is dropped without any error, which is a notorious silent-data-loss bug when two parallel lists drift out of sync. Python 3.10+ added zip(..., strict=True) to make length mismatches raise. enumerate(..., start=1) only changes the numbering, not the pairing.

questions.prompt: This should remove every even number, but drop_evens([1, 2, 2, 3]) returns [1, 2, 3]. What is the bug?
choices: remove() shifts later elements left while the loop's cursor advances, so the item right after each removal is never examined
remove() deletes the last occurrence of the value, not the first
n % 2 == 0 is unreliable when the list contains duplicate values
Lists silently ignore remove() calls made inside a for loop
questions.explain: The for loop walks positions 0, 1, 2... while remove() shifts everything after the deleted item one slot left — so the second 2 slides into the just-visited position and is skipped. Never mutate a list you are iterating; build a new one ([n for n in nums if n % 2]) or iterate over a copy. The same rule applies to dicts, which raise RuntimeError instead of failing silently.

questions.prompt: Both calls return a dict containing BOTH keys — a is {'hp': 10, 'mp': 5}. What is the bug?
questions.code:
def remember(key, value, cache={}):
    cache[key] = value
    return cache

a = remember("hp", 10)
b = remember("mp", 5)
choices: The default dict is created once at def time, so every call that omits cache shares and mutates the same object
return cache returns a live view that merges automatically with previous returns
Dict arguments are always global in Python functions
The bug is in the calls: keyword arguments are required for dict parameters
questions.explain: Same disease as the mutable-default list: the {} is evaluated once when def runs, and that single dict lives on between calls. Sometimes this is even used deliberately as a cheap cache — but an accidental version leaks state across requests, which in a web service means one user's data appearing in another's response. Default to cache=None plus an explicit 'if cache is None' guard.

questions.prompt: tally(['a', 'b']) crashes immediately. What is wrong?
choices: counts[w] on a key that is not yet present raises KeyError; use counts.get(w, 0) + 1, setdefault, or collections.Counter
Strings must be hashed explicitly with hash(w) before use as dict keys
+= cannot be used on dict values; it must be written counts[w] = counts[w] + 1
The dict needs to be pre-populated with every possible word mapped to 0
questions.explain: counts[w] += 1 reads counts[w] first, and the first time a word appears there is nothing to read — KeyError. The three idiomatic fixes are counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1, counts.setdefault(w, 0) followed by counts[w] += 1, or just collections.Counter(words), which is what a reviewer would expect in real code. Knowing all three and when each reads best is a standard interview checkpoint.

questions.prompt: This works, but a reviewer flags it for large inputs. What is the accepted criticism?
choices: Strings are immutable, so each += may copy everything built so far — quadratic worst case; collect parts in a list and ''.join them
The \n characters accumulate as separate objects and leak memory
page += line mutates line as a side effect, corrupting the caller's list
join is required for correctness because += breaks on non-ASCII text
questions.explain: A str can never be modified, so conceptually every += allocates a new string and copies both halves — O(n²) total over n lines. CPython has a refcount trick that often makes += behave in-place, but it is an implementation detail that vanishes the moment a second reference exists; '\n'.join(lines) is guaranteed O(total length) and is what reviewers expect.

questions.prompt: is_quit sometimes returns False even when command == 'quit' is True. Why?
choices: is tests object identity, not equality — two equal strings need not be the same object; use == for value comparison
The string 'quit' is interned, so is always returns True and the bug must be elsewhere
is only works between variables, never against a literal
str.compare() is required for string comparison in Python 3
questions.explain: is asks 'same object in memory?', == asks 'equal value?'. CPython interns many string literals, so this bug often passes casual testing — then fails on a string built at runtime (e.g. input().strip()), which is exactly what makes it dangerous. Python 3.8+ even emits a SyntaxWarning for is against a literal. Reserve is for singletons: x is None.

questions.prompt: After calling with_defaults({'theme': 'dark'}, DEFAULTS), the module-level DEFAULTS dict itself now contains 'theme': 'dark'. Why?
questions.code:
def with_defaults(settings, defaults):
    merged = defaults
    merged.update(settings)
    return merged
choices: merged = defaults binds a second name to the same dict, so update() mutates the caller's DEFAULTS; copy first: merged = dict(defaults)
update() always modifies both the receiver and its argument
Assignment inside a function automatically makes module-level dicts global
Dict literals passed as arguments are cached between calls
questions.explain: Assignment never copies in Python — merged and defaults are two names for one dict, so update() corrupts the shared DEFAULTS for every future caller. This is the aliasing bug in its most expensive production form: a slowly-mutating global config. Fix with merged = dict(defaults) then update, or in 3.9+ simply return defaults | settings, which builds a new dict.

questions.prompt: The tests require first-appearance order and this fails intermittently. What is wrong?
choices: Sets do not preserve insertion order — iteration order depends on hashing; use list(dict.fromkeys(names)) for an ordered dedupe
list() shuffles its input by default for security reasons
set() keeps the last occurrence of each value, reversing the order
Nothing is wrong — sets preserve insertion order since Python 3.7
questions.explain: The 3.7 insertion-order guarantee is for dicts only; set iteration order is an artifact of hash values and table size, and for str keys it can even differ between runs (hash randomization). list(dict.fromkeys(names)) dedupes while keeping first-appearance order, in O(n). 'Order-dependent output built from a set' is a classic source of flaky tests in real codebases.

questions.prompt: True or false: in a Python script, x = 1000 followed by y = 1000 guarantees that x is y is True, because equal integers are always the same object.
questions.explain: False — identity of equal numbers is never a language guarantee. CPython happens to cache small ints (-5 to 256) and may fold constants within one code object, so 'is' on ints works just often enough to breed bugs before failing. The rule to say in an interview: == compares values, is compares identity, and is is only for singletons like None.

questions.prompt: True or false: for large collections, 'x in my_list' is O(n) while 'x in my_set' and 'key in my_dict' are O(1) on average.
questions.explain: True — a list scan compares element by element, while sets and dicts hash the key and jump straight to its bucket. This is the single highest-leverage micro-decision in everyday Python: a membership check inside a loop against a list turns O(n·m); pre-building a set makes it O(n+m). At 100k elements the difference is roughly four orders of magnitude per lookup.

questions.prompt: True or false: since Python 3.7 the language guarantees that dicts iterate in insertion order.
questions.explain: True — it became a CPython implementation detail in 3.6 (the compact-dict layout) and an official language guarantee in 3.7, which is why plain dict has largely replaced OrderedDict. Two cautions for production: insertion order is not sorted order, and the guarantee does not extend to sets.

questions.prompt: True or false: Python's sort is stable — elements that compare equal keep their original relative order — so you can sort by a secondary key first and a primary key second to get a multi-level sort.
questions.explain: True — Timsort (used by both list.sort and sorted) guarantees stability, and the sort-by-secondary-then-primary trick depends on it. The other standard technique is a single pass with a tuple key, e.g. key=lambda w: (-w.count, w.word) for 'count descending, then word ascending' — expect an interviewer to ask for exactly that.

questions.prompt: True or false: any tuple can be used as a dictionary key, because tuples are immutable.
questions.explain: False — a dict key must be hashable, and a tuple is only hashable if everything inside it is: ([1], 2) raises TypeError because the list inside can change, which would silently break the hash table. Tuple immutability is shallow (it freezes the slots, not the contents). Tuples of strings/numbers make excellent composite keys, e.g. cache[(user_id, page)].
